segments.text: Senator from Utah.
Mr.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: President, the budget deal before the Senate today
is not just a

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: horrible piece of legislation that is undeserving of this Chamber's support.
It also represents the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: last gasping breath of a disgraced bipartisan Beltway establishment
on the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: verge of collapse.
The bill is

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the product of an unfair, dysfunctional,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: and fundamentally undemocratic process, a process that is virtually indistinguishable from

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: what we promised the American people, a GOP-controlled Congress, would bring to
an end.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: We made that promise precisely because negotiating legislation behind closed doors, without input from the majority of members,
and

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: then rushing it through to final passage without debate or opportunity for amendments violates our party's core principles. It also inevitably leads to bad policy. The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015 is a case in point. This bill would suspend the debt limit for 17 months and increase government spending beyond its already unsustainable levels.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: And it would do so, while failing to make reforms, that would put us on a path toward fiscal sustainability. Many proponents of this budget deal challenge this claim. They say, well, the bill isn't perfect, but while it isn't perfect, it does include some meaningful entitlement reforms. The sales pitch we hear most often alleges
that

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: This budget deal will save the Social Security Disability Trust Fund from insolvency. But we're never told exactly how this bill would do this. That's because, as always, the devil is in the details. Now, Mr. President, I rise today to discuss these very details, details that prove this budget deal's so-called entitlement reforms are nothing of the sort.
At best,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: they're well-intentioned but ineffectual tweaks to a program that desperately needs fundamental structural

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: overhaul. At worst, they're accounting gimmicks,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: unbecoming, of the United States Congress. According to the Social Security

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: Trustees,
the Social

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: Security Disability Insurance Program, or SSDI, is scheduled to run out of money in 2016.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: which means that without serious reform, disability benefits would be slashed across the board by nearly 20%.
Under

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015, the bankruptcy deadline of SSDI would be pushed off for an additional six years until 2022. But here's the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: kicker. It would do so by raiding the Social Security Trust Fund to the tune of $150 billion.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: That's right, our grand bipartisan solution to the impending insolvency of our nation's largest disability insurance program amounts to stealing $150 billion from our nation's largest retirement insurance program. And this isn't the only phony pay-for in this budget deal. There are others that simply

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: move around money from elsewhere in the federal budget, like the Crime Victims Fund and the Asset Forfeiture Fund.
There are

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: also new heavy-handed bureaucratic instruments that purport to implement cost savings in Medicaid

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: reimbursements, but really only impose misguided price controls on the generic drug

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: industry. Only in Washington, D.C. could something so deceptive and ineffective, something so unfair to America's seniors and future generations, be considered a reform.
There

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: are a couple of sound entitlement reforms in this budget deal that deserve to be commended. First, there is a provision that would correct a design error in the Social Security program that amounts to an unfair and wasteful loophole. Fixing this would save

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: a significant amount of money over a 75-year
window. There

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: are also measures that would increase the penalties for fraud, create new pilot programs, and prohibit doctors with

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: felonies from submitting medical evidence.
But

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: these minor changes don't even come close to putting SSDI on a path toward fiscal sustainability and sanity. And they represent

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_11
segments.text: only a tiny fraction of the sensible reform proposals put forth by

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: our conference. Many of my colleagues, like Senator Lankford and Senator Cotton, have already spoken or will soon speak.
on

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: the floor about the long list of structural reform ideas that are still sitting on the sidelines of this debate.
I'd like

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: to take a moment to touch on just a few of them. Senator Coates has a proposal that would protect the SSDI Trust Fund from being drawn down by fugitive felons illegally receiving disability benefits.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Senator Hatch has put forth a plan that would prevent an individual from receiving both unemployment insurance and disability insurance simultaneously, ensuring that SSDI funds would remain

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: focused on their intended population.
I also have

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: a proposal that would expand the footprint of private disability

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: insurance, which I intend to file as an amendment to this
bill. And

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: that's not all.
My friends,

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: Senator Cotton and Senator Lankford have their own proposals, and there have been an equal amount of policy innovation by our colleagues in the House of Representatives. They're all common sense ideas that would bring us much closer to real SSDI reform than

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: what's found in this budget deal. But you won't hear much about them in this debate, because there won't be any real debate the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2015.
No

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_04
segments.text: amendments, a fast approaching deadline, and in the end a take-it-or-leave-it choice forced upon us on our

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_12
segments.text: backs up against a cliff.
This is not how

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_12
segments.text: Congress is supposed to operate. This is not how we

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: promised the country we would conduct the American people's business if given control of the House and the Senate. We should be the party of ideas.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: But we won't be, so long as we continue to tolerate a legislative process that stifles our most innovative proposals from even getting a fair hearing. We should be the party of reform, but we won't be, so long as individual senators are blocked from offering amendments to legislation. We should be the party of fiscal sanity and responsible governance, but we won't be so long as we continue to govern
by

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: crisis and by cliff, delaying the inevitable while working

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: only three days a week in our legislative calendar. We should be the party that looks out for the most vulnerable among us, but we won't be so long as we lack the courage to enact the

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_05
segments.text: structural reforms that our retirement and disability insurance programs need to survive

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: for generations
to come.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_03
segments.text: Mr. President, we can be all of these things. I know we can. But it's going to take hard
work
A

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_00
segments.text: fair, open, and inclusive legislative process, and all the policy innovation we can muster. It's going to take something

segments.speaker: SPEAKER_06
segments.text: more, something better, than this budget deal. I yield the floor.
